title: J. van Zuylen (1981) The microscopes of Antoni van Leeuwenhoek, J. Microscopy 121:309-328
facts: realistic formula for smallest resolvable detail under uncontrolled lighting: d = lambda/(1.3 NA); with good modern lenses and carefully adjusted central illumination a factor 1.7 can be attained
only very few older biconvex lenses surpass the factor 1.5, most fall markedly behind, even 0.5 is possible (Van der Star 1953 measurements)

practical limit for spherical aberration: centre intensity of the disc diminished to 80% (equivalent to Rayleigh limit); beyond 3x Rayleigh limit loss of contrast requires restricting the illuminating aperture; with parallel light useful images up to 20x Rayleigh limit but resolving power no longer increases
calculated resolving powers in Table 1 use the aperture at which spherical aberration equals 2-5x the Rayleigh limit

a biconvex lens with 0.5 mm free aperture, NA 0.30, spherical aberration 2.5x Rayleigh limit, is close to optimal for a simple microscope and should resolve 1.17 um; a glass sphere of radius 0.54 mm at NA 0.315 should resolve 1.11 um
Utrecht resolving power 1.42 um measured by Harting (1850) and Van Cittert with the same Nobert test plate
Rayleigh criterion: contrast between max and min at least 26% lower than the maximum; r = 0.61 lambda/NA
r = lambda/(2NA) common in microscopy literature; with condenser r = 1.22 lambda/(NA_obj + NA_cond)
bar-target limiting resolution measures the contrast transfer function (CTF), not the MTF
Nobert's ruled test gratings began in 1840 with ten lines, extended to 20 divisions in 1851 and thirty in 1855; sold for about 5 Thalers in 1846
finest lines of Nobert's plates were found to be at a distance of 0.1128 um (Turner & Bradbury 1966)
